issues.legal_issue: A judgment debtor must receive notice before decree holders are permitted to bid at an execution sale at a price below the previously fixed upset price.
material_facts: The decree holders sought permission to bid at the execution sale.
The executing court permitted them to bid at a price equal to 80 per cent of the previously fixed upset price without notice to the judgment debtor.
issues.conclusion: Notice to the judgment debtor is necessary before permission is granted to bid at a reduced upset price.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 21, Rule 72 of the Code of Civil Procedure, notice to the judgment debtor is necessary before permission is granted to decree holders to bid, particularly when the upset price is proposed to be reduced. The Court agreed with the submission supported by G. Subramania Mudaliar v. The Ideal Finance Corporation, Partnership Firm and Puttaparatti Atchamma v. T. Bayanna.

predicates.execution_sale_proceeding: A court is conducting a sale to enforce a decree.
predicates.decree_holders_seek_bid_permission: The decree holders ask the court for permission to bid at the sale.
predicates.proposed_bid_price_below_upset_price: The permission sought would allow bidding at a price below the previously fixed upset price.

issues.definition: When decree holders seek permission to bid below the previously fixed upset price in an execution sale, the judgment debtor must receive notice before permission is granted.

issues.legal_issue: An irregularity in the conduct of an execution sale does not justify setting it aside unless the applicant proves that the irregularity caused substantial injury.
material_facts: The decree holders purchased the property at the court auction after receiving permission to bid at a reduced price without notice to the judgment debtor.
The judgment debtor challenged the sale under Order 21, Rule 90, relying on the absence of notice.
The Court found no sufficient facts showing that the absence of notice caused substantial injury to the judgment debtor.
issues.conclusion: The application to set aside the sale was properly rejected because substantial injury resulting from the irregularity was not proved.
issues.legal_principle: Order 21, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires an applicant challenging an execution sale to prove not only an illegality or material irregularity in the conduct of the sale but also substantial injury caused by it. The Court found no material irregularity or illegality vitiating the sale under the applicable provisions and upheld the rejection of the application.

rule.if: execution_sale_set_aside_application and sale_conduct_irregularity and not substantial_injury_caused_by_irregularity

predicates.execution_sale_set_aside_application: A person applies to have a sale conducted to enforce a decree set aside.
predicates.sale_conduct_irregularity: An irregularity occurred in the conduct of the execution sale.
predicates.substantial_injury_caused_by_irregularit: The irregularity caused substantial injury to the person challenging the sale.

issues.definition: An application challenging an execution sale fails when an irregularity occurred but did not cause substantial injury.
